findings.source_quote: οἶμαι δὲ ἐκ τοῦ πλείστου τελευτῆσαι αὐτόν
findings.english_quote: I think he has most likely died
findings.issue: ἐκ τοῦ πλείστου is naturally understood here as grounding the inference in the long elapsed time. The draft instead makes it a probability modifier. Its note neither preserves the material temporal alternative nor establishes why “most likely” is preferable; observing that the death is inferred does not distinguish these readings.
findings.suggested_revision: Propose “I think he has died, given how long it has been,” with a note explaining the implicit temporal reference. If retaining “most likely,” substantiate that lexical reading and disclose the elapsed-time alternative with a contextual rationale. The revised text and note require fresh review; this is an interpretive issue, not evidence of source corruption.

findings.source_quote: καὶ καταφιλήσαντες ἦγον ἐπὶ τὴν ξενίαν
findings.english_quote: embraced us with kisses, and led us to our lodging
findings.issue: καταφιλήσαντες describes affectionate kissing, not a separate embrace. The English introduces an additional physical gesture. Elsewhere in these passages the source explicitly distinguishes embracing from kissing.
findings.suggested_revision: Propose “kissed us warmly and led us to our lodging,” without adding an embrace.

findings.source_quote: ἢ ἄλλος τις ἐκ φύσεως στοργὴν ἔχων
findings.english_quote: or anyone else for whom one has natural affection
findings.issue: The active participle ἔχων makes the other person the holder of the natural affection. The draft reverses that relationship, making the person its recipient and introducing an unspecified “one” as its holder. Reciprocal family affection may be contextually plausible, but it does not justify replacing the source's stated relationship.
findings.suggested_revision: Propose “or anyone else who feels natural affection,” leaving the affection's object unexpressed as in the Greek.

findings.issue: The superlative or elative intensity of χαλεπωτάτῃ is not distinctly represented. The draft later renders the positive χαλεπὴν as “terrible,” leaving the source's earlier intensification effectively flattened.
findings.suggested_revision: Propose “on that extremely dreadful night” to preserve elative intensity without requiring a uniquely worst night, or “on that most dreadful night” if retaining the superlative form. Keep the later positive expression distinct. The replacement requires fresh review.
